question: What happens to an employee's status under the Canada Labour Code if they cease to work due to a lockout or strike, or are dismissed contrary to the Code?
answer:
## Employee Status During Lockouts and Strikes, and Dismissals Contrary to the Code

### Rights Unaffected During Lockouts and Strikes

Section 87.5 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the status of employees during lockouts and strikes, emphasizing that their rights are not affected unless the bargaining agent consents to changes in terms and conditions of employment.
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This section explicitly states that an employer cannot unilaterally alter an employee's terms and conditions of employment during a lockout or strike without the bargaining agent's consent. This ensures that employees retain their existing rights and privileges until the dispute is resolved.

### Reinstatement of Employees After Strike or Lockout

Section 87.6 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's obligation to reinstate employees after a strike or lockout.
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person."

This provision mandates that employers must reinstate employees who were on strike or locked out, giving them preference over any other potential hires. This ensures that employees who participated in the strike or lockout are restored to their previous employment status.

### Dismissals Contrary to the Code

While the provided documents do not directly address dismissals contrary to the Code, Section 87.5 indirectly touches upon this issue by stating that employers cannot alter terms and conditions of employment without the bargaining agent's consent until the Board makes a determination. This implies that dismissals that violate the Code's requirements regarding terms and conditions of employment would be subject to the Board's review and potential reversal.

Furthermore, Section 87.6's reinstatement requirement reinforces the protection afforded to employees who participated in a strike or lockout. Dismissals that occur in retaliation for such participation would likely be deemed contrary to the Code.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Anti-reprisal protection for  concerted activity** Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal. This is particularly true for non-unionized workers and  those in non-standard work, as well as women. For instance, using survey  data collected in 2005, Lewchuk (2013) concludes that "the precariously  employed were six to seven times more likely to report that raising health and  safety issues would have negative employment consequences".  In the United States, section 7 of the National Labor  Relations Act (NLRA) provides non-supervisory employees, both union and  non-union, with the right to engage in "concerted activity for the purpose of  collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection". As defined by the  U.S. Supreme Court, "mutual aid and protection" includes employees’ efforts to  "improve current terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their  lots as employees through channels outside the immediate employee/employer  relationship"Footnote 135 The Act does not limit the manner, time or place in which  employees engage in "concerted activity". While section 7 lists workers’ protected rights, section 8 makes it  unlawful for an employer to "interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in  the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7". The employer’s conduct will be considered as retaliation if  it tends to interfere with the free exercise of employee rights under the NLRA  and "demonstrating motive or actual coercion is therefore not generally  required" (Rogers & Archer, 2016). Sections 7 and 8 were introduced  when the NLRA was enacted in 1935.  Section 7 of the NLRA protects concerted activities by  unionized workers and non-unionized workers, whether they are seeking to  unionize or not (Rogers & Archer, 2016). The spectrum of protected  concerted activities is wide and includes concerted complaints or grievances  presented to employers regarding compensation, benefits or working conditions,  as well as informal discussions between employees about their working  conditions (Fullerton & Millman, 2008). The protected activities must generally be undertaken by two or more  employees seeking to improve their terms or conditions of employment.  Thus, two or more employees addressing their employer about  improving their pay will be exercising their right to protected concerted  activity. However, the  protection can also extend to the actions of one employee, on the condition  that such actions have "the object of initiating or inducing or preparing  for group action or [have] some relation to group action in the interest of the  employees." Footnote 136 Footnote 137 Section 7 will apply when an  employee speaks to his employer on behalf of one or more co-workers about  improving workplace conditions (NLRB, n.d.). Non-union work stoppages and  walkouts are generally protected,Footnote 138 unless they are "unlawful, violent, […] in breach of contract [or]  "irresponsible" because they threaten property damage" (Rogers & Archer,  2016). Section 7 has been interpreted to  extend the "Weingarten" rule (that is, that an employee in a  unionized workplace may request the presence of a union representative at an  investigatory interview which employee reasonably believes might result in  disciplinary action) to cover employees in non-union workplaces.Footnote 139 The use of social media is, to a  certain extent, protected by section 7 as employees have the right to address  work-related issues and share information about pay, benefits, and working  conditions with coworkers on Facebook, YouTube, and other social media. To be  protected, the use of social media must have some relation to group action, or  seek to initiate, induce or prepare for group action, or bring a group  complaint to the attention of management (Neylon O’Brien, 2011; Bemberg, 2018).  For  instance, an employer's decision to  dismiss an employee who posted a comment on Facebook encouraging a terminated  colleague to hire a lawyer and sue the company was over-ruled by the National  Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The Facebook comment was found to be a protected concerted activity  that did not interfere with the employer’s operations.Footnote 140 However, complaints that are made  publicly and are maliciously false will not be protected.Footnote 141 Many employers have social media policies that aim to limit what their  employee may publish. When such policies are found to be overly broad (that is,  when they prohibit lawful activities either explicitly or by being too vague),  the NLRB can order the employer to rescind or modify them.Footnote 142 Protected  concerted activities provide statutory protection against reprisals for  employees wishing to collectively voice concerns. This form of collective voice  is independent from the employer who is required to not interfere. The American  experience suggests that it can be useful in circumstances in which employees  face particularly egregious working conditions and are otherwise unable to  bring about change or improvements.  For  example, in a leading 1962 case (NLRB v. Washington  Aluminum) workers had  complained about the cold temperatures in the facility during the winter. Footnote 143 On a particularly cold day workers arrived to  find the plant completely unheated and seven walked out. The U.S. Supreme Court  upheld the NLRB’s ruling that the company’s termination of these workers was  unlawful. Similarly, in a more recent case a group of restaurant workers who  had been terminated after protesting working conditions appealed to the NLRB  which ordered them reinstated (Greenhouse, 2015). A search on Lexis Advance US conducted in March  2019 yielded 8,993 NLRB cases dealing with section 7, going back as far as  1935. Although this is a small number over a period of more than 80 years, the  number of cases per year has grown substantially in recent years during a time  when private sector unionization has also fallen sharply. Figure 18  plots  the number of cases per year over the 1935 to 2019 period. The number has  increased significantly over the past two decades.   Figure 18: Number of cases before the NLRB  (section 7 NLRA), 1935–2019   Figure 18 - Text version    Dates Number of cases   1935–1939 396   1940–1944 487   1945–1949 24   1950–1954 42   1955–1959 45   1960–1964 102   1965–1969 187   1970–1974 430   1975-1979 916   1980–1984 854   1985–1989 445   1990–1994 443   1995–1999 329   2000–2004 335   2005-2009 753   2010–2014 1806   2015–2019 1565      Source:  Panel analysis of NLRB/Lexis Advance US.    However, it is important to note that the number of cases  related to section 7 is likely to understate the importance of this provision  because of the "threat effect"—employers who are aware of the law and previous  interpretations by the courts will adjust their behaviour in order to be in  compliance and avoid a costly lawsuit.  Unlike some other  mechanisms, the NLRA protection for concerted activity has the advantage of  having been available and used in the United States, a country that shares many  commonalities with Canada’s labour relations system. It is unclear whether the  collective voice achievable with the support of such a protection might develop  into more sustained collective activity, such as achieving union  representation. Nevertheless, adopting a protection for concerted activity  might be helpful for workers in the FRPS with particularly poor working  conditions.  Recommendation 25: The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such  reprisals.Footnote 144 Adding a protection for  concerted activity to Part III would also likely enhance workers’  willingness to join participatory initiatives channelled through community  organizations. The Panel views this right as a potentially useful incremental  change to Canada’s labour relations system in the FRPS and one that would bring  the Code more in line with recent Supreme Court interpretations of the  guarantee of freedom of association in section 2(d) of the Canadian Charter of  Rights and Freedoms."

question: How does the Canada Labour Code ensure that the rights provided under the Canadian Human Rights Act are protected in the context of employment relationships?
answer:
## Protection of Canadian Human Rights Act Rights within Employment Relationships under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 123.1 of the Canada Labour Code
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act..."

This statement, found in Section 123.1 of the Canada Labour Code, directly addresses the question of how the Code ensures the protection of rights provided under the Canadian Human Rights Act. It establishes a fundamental principle: the Canada Labour Code is not intended to diminish or conflict with the protections offered by the Canadian Human Rights Act. Instead, it operates alongside and in support of those broader human rights guarantees. This ensures that the rights enshrined in the Canadian Human Rights Act remain fully operative within the context of employment relationships, even as the Canada Labour Code addresses specific labour standards.

### Section 123.2: Presumption of Employee Status and Burden of Proof
"...section 7 of the National Labor  Relations Act (NLRA) provides non-supervisory employees, both union and  non-union, with the right to engage in "concerted activity for the purpose of  collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection". As defined by the  U.S. Supreme Court, "mutual aid and protection" includes employees’ efforts to  "improve current terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their  lots as employees through channels outside the immediate employee/employer..."

While this section primarily discusses the rights of employees under the US National Labor Relations Act, it is relevant to understanding the broader context of protected concerted activity. The principle that employees have the right to engage in collective action to improve their working conditions is a cornerstone of labour law in both Canada and the United States. The Canada Labour Code, by incorporating protections for concerted activity, aligns with this principle and ensures that employees can exercise their rights to mutual aid and protection without fear of reprisal.

### Section 123.3: Burden of Proof in Reprisal Cases
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This provision within Section 123.3 of the Canada Labour Code is crucial for safeguarding human rights. It establishes a clear legal principle regarding the burden of proof in cases of reprisal. If an employer attempts to argue that an employee is not their employee in order to justify a retaliatory action, the employer bears the responsibility of proving this claim. This protects employees from being penalized for exercising their human rights, such as speaking out about workplace safety concerns or engaging in collective action to improve their working conditions.

### Recommendation 25: Introducing Protection for Concerted Activities in Part III
"The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such..."

This recommendation, made by the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards, directly addresses the question of protecting human rights within employment relationships. It proposes adding a specific provision to Part III of the Canada Labour Code that explicitly recognizes employees' right to participate in concerted activities. Furthermore, it recommends providing protection against reprisal for employees who exercise this right. This would ensure that employees are not penalized for engaging in collective action to improve their working conditions, thereby reinforcing the protections offered by the Canadian Human Rights Act.

question: What protections are afforded to the Head and those delegated authority under the Canada Labour Code when carrying out their duties and functions?
answer:
## Protections Afforded to the Head and Those Delegated Authority

### Section 249: Liability and Evidence Preclusion

#### Section 249(7) and (8): Immunity from Testimony and Personal Liability
"The Head shall not be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions." This section explicitly states that the Head is not obligated to provide testimony in civil cases concerning information gathered while performing their duties. This protection shields the Head from potential legal scrutiny based on information obtained during inspections or other investigative activities.
"Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part." This provision extends immunity to those to whom the Head has delegated authority. It clarifies that neither the Head nor the delegate is personally responsible for any actions taken in good faith under the authority granted by this Part. This protection is crucial for those carrying out the Head's duties, as it safeguards them from potential legal repercussions arising from their actions taken in accordance with the Head's instructions.

### Section 249(4): Reasonable Assistance
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations." This section mandates that all personnel within federal workplaces must provide the Head with "all reasonable assistance" to facilitate the Head's performance of their duties. This protection ensures that the Head has the necessary support to carry out their responsibilities effectively, without undue obstruction or hindrance.

### Section 272: Delegation and Immunity
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate." This section reiterates the Head's power to delegate authority, and it includes a protection for both the Head and the delegates. The Head is not personally liable for actions taken by those to whom they have delegated authority, provided those actions are taken in good faith under the Head's instructions. Furthermore, the Head is not required to testify in civil proceedings regarding information obtained by the delegates while carrying out their delegated duties.

question: Can the Commission unilaterally impose new safety standards on coal mines, or does it require input or applications from employers?
answer:
## Coal Mining Safety Commission: Imposing New Safety Standards

### Section 137.2(1) - Commission Approval of Plans and Procedures
"The Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)."

This section indicates that the Commission does not unilaterally impose new safety standards. Instead, it operates on an approval basis. Employers must submit plans and procedures for any activity for which such submission is prescribed, and the Commission has the authority to approve these plans, with or without modifications. This implies that the Commission requires input and applications from employers before new safety standards can be implemented.

### Section 137.2(2) - Commission Approval of Alternative Methods, Machinery, and Equipment
"On the application of an employer, the Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, (a) approve in writing the use by the employer in coal mines of mining methods, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable; or (b) approve in writing, notwithstanding anything in this Part, the use by the employer in coal mines, for a specified time and subject to specified conditions, of any mining method, machinery or equipment that does not meet prescribed safety standards applicable in respect of it."

This subsection further clarifies the Commission's role in safety standards. It allows employers to apply for approval to use mining methods, machinery, or equipment that do not meet prescribed safety standards. The Commission can grant this approval if it deems that the protection of employee health and safety would not be diminished. This demonstrates that the Commission does not unilaterally impose new safety standards but rather provides a mechanism for employers to seek exceptions or alternative approaches, subject to the Commission's approval.

### Section 137.2(3) - Commission Exemptions and Substitutions
"On the application of an employer, the Commission may, if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, by order, (a) exempt the employer from compliance with any provision of the regulations in the operation of coal mines controlled by the employer, subject to any conditions contained in the order; or (b) substitute for any provision of the regulations, so far as it applies to coal mines controlled by the employer, another provision having substantially the same purpose and effect."

This subsection provides the Commission with the power to grant exemptions or substitute provisions of the regulations at the request of an employer, provided that it believes employee health and safety would not be compromised. This indicates that the Commission does not unilaterally impose new safety standards but rather allows for adjustments to existing standards through employer applications and the Commission's subsequent approval.

### Section 137.2(4) - Commission Recommendations for Amendments
"The Commission may make recommendations to the Minister for amending or revoking any provision of the regulations applicable to coal mines or for adding any provision thereto."

This section highlights the Commission's role in suggesting changes to the regulations. It can make recommendations to the Minister for amendments or additions. This implies that the Commission does not unilaterally impose new safety standards but rather initiates the process of regulatory changes through recommendations to the Minister.

In conclusion, the Coal Mining Safety Commission does not unilaterally impose new safety standards on coal mines. It operates on an approval basis, requiring input and applications from employers for any deviations from prescribed safety standards. The Commission then reviews these applications and makes decisions on whether to approve them, grant exemptions, or recommend regulatory changes to the Minister.

question: How does referencing Section 189 in Section 237 of the Canada Labour Code affect the application of this Division?
answer:
## Section 189's Application in Section 237 of the Canada Labour Code

### General Application of Section 189

Section 237 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states:
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This indicates a direct and broad application of Section 189 to the entire Division concerning severance pay.

### How Section 189 Affects Severance Pay

Section 189 deals with the continuity of employment in the context of lease or transfer of work, undertaking, or business. It establishes a principle for determining whether an employee's period of continuous employment is linked to one employer or another following such a transaction.

The text of Section 189 is crucial to understanding its effect on severance pay. It states:
"For greater certainty, if an employer’s work, undertaking or business becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to a change in its activities, for the purposes of this Division, an employee’s period of continuous employment by the employer includes any period in which the work, undertaking or business in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed was not a federal work, undertaking or business."

This passage is directly relevant to Section 237 because it clarifies how the continuity of employment principle applies to situations where an employer's work becomes federal. In the context of severance pay, this means that if an employer's work transitions to federal status, an employee's continuous employment with the first employer is not disrupted for the purpose of calculating their severance entitlement under Section 235.

Furthermore, Section 189 includes exceptions that are also pertinent to severance pay. It states:
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of the employee’s entitlement under section 230 if the first employer complied with that section in respect of their employment by that employer." This means that if the first employer complied with Section 230 (which deals with the calculation of severance pay), the continuity of employment principle under Section 189 does not affect the calculation of severance pay under Section 230 when the employee is employed by the second employer.

In essence, referencing Section 189 in Section 237 ensures that the continuity of employment principle established in Section 189 is applied consistently across the entire Division concerning severance pay, taking into account various scenarios such as lease/transfer of business and changes in employer status.

## Governor in Council's Power to Extend Part III Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

### Section 158 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section directly addresses the question. It explicitly states that the Governor in Council has the authority to extend the application of Part III of the Canada Labour Code to employment within corporations that function as agents of a province and whose activities are subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. The phrase "direct that this Part applies" indicates a clear power to broaden the scope of Part III's application. The inclusion of
"...including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." clarifies that this extension applies even to corporations operating under the specific regulatory framework of the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section reiterates the power of the Governor in Council to extend Part III's application to provincial Crown corporations involved in activities regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It uses similar language to Section 158, emphasizing the ability to "direct that this Part applies" to such employment. The repetition reinforces the clarity of this provision regarding the Governor in Council's authority.

### Section 121.1 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section provides yet another instance of the Governor in Council's power to extend Part III's application to provincial Crown corporations operating under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It employs the same phrasing as Sections 158 and 265, confirming the breadth of this regulatory authority. The inclusion of this section further solidifies the answer.

question: What is the intended effect of setting a time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 161 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Section 161: Pilot Projects - Time Limit for Validity of Regulations

### Intended Effect of Setting a Time Limit

Section 161 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations concerning the establishment and operation of pilot projects. These projects are designed to test potential amendments to the Part or its regulations to improve accident, injury, and illness prevention in employment covered by this Part. A time limit is set for the validity of these regulations to ensure that the pilot projects remain relevant and that the findings are timely for potential future amendments.

The text explicitly states,
"(g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit..." This indicates that the time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 161 is linked to the time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 99.01(1). The purpose of this time limit is to provide a framework for the pilot projects and their outcomes.

Furthermore, the section emphasizes the need for the pilot projects to be adaptable. It mentions,
"...and adapting any such provision for the purposes of that application." This suggests that the time limit is intended to allow for the evaluation of the pilot projects and the potential adaptation of the regulations based on their findings before the regulations expire.

In essence, setting a time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 161 serves to create a dynamic process for improving workplace safety. It ensures that the pilot projects are conducted within a relevant timeframe and that the regulations are updated based on the project's results before they become outdated.

question: What is the overall purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under this section of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Overall Purpose of Regulations Made Under Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code

### Broad Scope of Regulatory Authority

Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad regulatory authority. The overall purpose of these regulations is to "carry out the purposes of this Part" and to address any other matters
"...that under this Part is required or permitted to be prescribed by regulation." This indicates a flexible framework allowing for detailed rules and procedures to be established to support the broader objectives of the Canada Labour Code.

### Key Areas Addressed by Regulations

The regulations outlined in Section 264 cover a wide range of labour standards and administrative matters. These can be broadly categorized as follows:

#### Record-Keeping Requirements

Regulations can mandate employers to maintain specific records related to employee wages, vacations, holidays, overtime, and other relevant details. This ensures transparency and facilitates compliance with labour laws. For instance, it states:
"...requiring employers to keep records relevant to the purposes of this Part in respect of persons who are excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of all or any of this Part..."
This highlights the ability to tailor record-keeping requirements to specific employment situations.

#### Information Provision to the Head

Regulations can specify the information employers must provide to the Head of the federal government to demonstrate compliance with certain programs. This allows for oversight and verification of employer practices. It specifies:
"...respecting the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it..."
This demonstrates the power to define the scope and timing of information reporting.

#### Wage Calculation and Determination

Regulations can prescribe methods for calculating and determining regular wages, including hourly rates and wages paid on commission or salary plus commission. This ensures fair compensation for employees. It details:
"...for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees..."
This underscores the ability to establish specific wage calculation rules.

#### Hours of Work and Rest Periods

Regulations can set maximum daily working hours and prescribe requirements for rest and meal periods. This aims to protect employee health and safety. It states:
"...prescribing the maximum number of hours that may elapse between the commencement and termination of the working day of any employee..."
This illustrates the capacity to establish specific limits on working hours.

#### Notice and Reporting Procedures

Regulations can detail the form, content, and manner in which notices and reports must be given or sent to the Minister or other relevant parties. This ensures proper communication and record-keeping. It specifies:
"...prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining..."
This demonstrates the ability to establish specific requirements for certain types of notices.

#### Administrative Matters

Regulations can address various administrative aspects, such as the designation of industrial establishments, the establishment of consultative committees, and the procedures for filing orders and decisions. This provides a framework for the effective administration of the Canada Labour Code. It mentions:
"...providing for the establishment of consultative or advisory committees to advise the Minister on any matters arising in relation to the administration of this Part..."
This highlights the ability to create advisory bodies to support the Minister's work.

### Exclusion from Application

Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code specifically addresses the exclusion of certain employment from the application of this Part. The Governor in Council can, by regulation, exclude employment based on the nature of the work or undertaking, particularly those regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This allows for the tailoring of labour standards to specific sectors. It states:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment..."
This directly addresses the power to create exemptions from the general labour standards.

In summary, the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code serve a comprehensive purpose: to provide detailed rules and procedures to effectively implement and administer the broader labour standards outlined in this Part of the Canada Labour Code. They address a wide range of issues, from record-keeping to wage calculation to administrative processes, while also allowing for the tailoring of standards to specific sectors through the power of exclusion.

question: How can The Board ensure that the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, its regulations, and its decisions are complied with?
answer:
## Ensuring Compliance with the Canada Labour Code

### Powers and Duties of the Board to Ensure Compliance

The Board possesses a wide array of powers and duties specifically designed to ensure compliance with the Canada Labour Code, its regulations, and its decisions. These powers span from investigative measures to enforcement actions and the issuance of orders.

#### Assisting Parties to Settle Complaints and Determining Complaints
"...on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint." This passage highlights the Board's initial role in facilitating voluntary compliance. By assisting parties to settle complaints, the Board aims to resolve issues amicably and ensure adherence to the Code without resorting to more forceful measures. However, if settlement fails, the Board has the authority to formally determine the complaint, which can lead to various enforcement actions.

#### Summoning Witnesses and Compelling Evidence
"The Board has, in relation to any proceeding before it, power (a) to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce such documents and things as the Board deems requisite to the full investigation and consideration of any matter within its jurisdiction that is before the Board in the proceeding..." This power is fundamental to the Board's ability to investigate potential non-compliance. By compelling witnesses to testify and produce documents, the Board can gather the necessary information to determine whether the Code, its regulations, or its decisions are being followed.

#### Issuing Orders and Requiring Compliance
"...the Board may, by order, require the party to comply with or cease contravening that subsection or section and may (a) in respect of a failure to comply with subsection 24(4), section 47.3, paragraph 50(b) or subsection 87.5(1) or (2) or 87.7(2), by order, require an employer to pay to any employee compensation not exceeding such sum as, in the opinion of the Board, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for that failure, have been paid by the employer to the employee; (a.1) in respect of a contravention of subsection 34(6), by order, require an employer representative to take and carry on on behalf of any employer affected by the contravention, or to assist any such employer to take and carry on, such action or proceeding as the Board considers that the representative ought to have taken and carried on on the employer’s behalf or ought to have assisted the employer to take and carry on; (b) in respect of a contravention of section 37, require a trade union to take and carry on on behalf of any employee affected by the contravention or to assist any such employee to take and carry on such action or proceeding as the Board considers that the union ought to have taken and carried on on the employee’s behalf or ought to have assisted the employee to take and carry on; (b.1) in respect of a contravention of the obligation to bargain collectively in good faith mentioned in paragraph 50(a), by order, require that an employer or a trade union include in or withdraw from a bargaining position specific terms or direct a binding method of resolving those terms, if the Board considers that this order is necessary to remedy the contravention or counteract its effects..." This section details the Board's ability to issue orders requiring compliance. These orders can mandate employers to pay compensation, implement workplace policies, reinstate employees, or cease non-compliance. The Board can also order unions to take specific actions to remedy violations.

#### Administrative and Monetary Penalties
"As of January 1, 2021, the Labour Program may issue a notice of violation with an administrative monetary penalty (AMP). The Labour Program may issue the notice if you do not correct a contravention of the Code..." This power allows the Board to impose financial penalties on employers who fail to comply with the Code or its regulations. The AMP serves as a deterrent and a means of compensating employees for losses incurred due to non-compliance.

#### Filing in Federal Court and Public Naming
"The Labour Program may file a payment order and a notice of violation in federal court to ensure that it is enforceable as a judgment of that court. The Labour Program may also publish information on the Government of Canada website concerning an employer to whom a payment order or notice of violation has been issued..." These actions enhance the Board's ability to enforce its orders and ensure compliance. Filing in court provides a legally binding mechanism for collecting unpaid wages or other compensation. Public naming of employers who violate the Code serves as a public warning and can pressure employers to comply.

#### Prosecutions
"If you do not correct a contravention with the Code or Regulations, the Labour Program may choose to prosecute you. The Labour Program may also take this route if you are fully aware of your legal obligations and still willfully break the law." Prosecutions represent the most severe enforcement action available to the Board. By pursuing criminal charges, the Board can impose significant fines and even imprisonment on employers who repeatedly or willfully violate the Code.

### Regulations and Powers of the Board to Develop and Enforce Compliance Mechanisms

#### Making Regulations
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings; (b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit; (f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit; (g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part; (n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union; (o) the circumstances in which evidence referred to in paragraph (m) may be received by the Board as evidence that any employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, including the circumstances in which the evidence so received by the Board may not be made public by the Board; (o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes; (p) the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions; (p.1) the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators; and (q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This section details the Board's power to create detailed rules and procedures for its operations. These regulations are crucial for ensuring fairness, efficiency, and consistency in the Board's enforcement efforts. They cover aspects like pre-hearing procedures, telecommunication use, bargaining unit determination, certification processes, representation votes, evidence presentation, and the selection of external adjudicators.

#### Adjourning and Postponing Proceedings
"...adjourn or postpone the proceeding from time to time..." This power allows the Board to manage its workload and ensure that proceedings are conducted fairly and efficiently.

#### Deciding Questions Arising in Proceedings
"...decide for all purposes of this Part any question that may arise in the proceeding, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any question as to whether (i) a person is an employer or an employee, (ii) a person performs management functions or is employed in a confidential capacity in matters relating to industrial relations, (iii) a person is a member of a trade union, (iv) an organization or association is an employers’ organization, a trade union or a council of trade unions, (v) a group of employees is a unit appropriate for collective bargaining, (vi) a collective agreement has been entered into, (vii) any person or organization is a party to or bound by a collective agreement, and (viii) a collective agreement is in operation..." question: What is the primary concern that the Canada Labour Code aims to address by allowing pregnant or nursing employees to request job modifications or reassignments?
answer:
## Primary Concern Addressed by Job Modifications and Reassignments for Pregnant/Nursing Employees

### Health Risks to Employee and Fetus/Child

The primary concern that the Canada Labour Code aims to address by allowing pregnant or nursing employees to request job modifications or reassignments is the potential health risks to the employee and the developing fetus or child. Section 204 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states:
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing may, during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, request the employer to modify her job functions or reassign her to another job if, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."

This section directly links the pregnancy or nursing condition to potential health risks. The Code recognizes that certain job functions may create conditions that could negatively impact the employee's health or the well-being of the child. Therefore, it provides a mechanism for employees to seek adjustments to their work to mitigate these risks.

### Employer's Obligation to Consider Requests

The Code further emphasizes the employer's responsibility to consider these requests. Section 205 outlines the employer's obligations:
"An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee’s job functions or reassign her."

This passage highlights that the employer is not simply permitted to deny these requests but must actively engage with the employee to explore reasonable accommodations. The phrase "where reasonably practicable" acknowledges that not all job modifications or reassignments may be feasible, but it underscores the employer's commitment to finding solutions that protect the employee's health and the child's well-being.

### Certificate Requirement for Justification

To ensure that job modifications or reassignments are necessary due to health risks, the Code mandates a certificate from a health care practitioner. Section 204(2) specifies:
"An employee’s request under subsection (1) must be accompanied by a certificate from a health care practitioner of the employee’s choice indicating the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk."

This requirement provides a medical basis for the request, ensuring that the adjustments are directly linked to a demonstrable health concern. The certificate helps to define the scope and duration of the potential risk, guiding the employer in determining appropriate accommodations.

In essence, the Canada Labour Code prioritizes the health and safety of pregnant or nursing employees and their children by empowering them to request job adjustments when their current work poses a risk. It also places a clear obligation on employers to seriously consider these requests and to work collaboratively with employees to find reasonable solutions.

question: How does the law ensure that employees receive the wages and compensation they are entitled to when an employer has been convicted of an offence related to non-payment or underpayment of wages?
answer:
## Ensuring Employees Receive Entitled Wages and Compensation After Employer Conviction

### Order to Pay Arrears of Wages

The Canada Labour Code outlines a mechanism through which employees can recover unpaid or underpaid wages after an employer has been convicted of an offence related to wage non-payment. Section 258(1) states:
"Where an employer has been convicted of an offence under this Part in respect of any employee, the convicting court shall, in addition to any other punishment, order the employer to pay to the employee any overtime pay, vacation pay, holiday pay or other wages or amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part the non-payment or insufficient payment of which constituted the offence for which the employer was convicted."

This provision mandates that the court, in addition to any other penalties imposed on the employer, will order the employer to pay the employee all wages and amounts to which they were legally entitled but were not paid in full. This ensures that employees receive the compensation they were owed as a direct consequence of the employer's conviction for wage violations.

### Compensation for Loss of Employment and Reinstatement

Furthermore, the law provides for compensation for loss of employment and reinstatement of the employee in their former position. Section 258(2) elaborates on this:
"Where an employer has been convicted of an offence under this Part in respect of the discharge of an employee, the convicting court may, in addition to any other punishment, order the employer (a) to pay compensation for loss of employment to the employee not exceeding such sum as in the opinion of the court is equivalent to the wages that would have accrued to the employee up to the date of conviction but for such discharge; and (b) to reinstate the employee in his employ at such date as in the opinion of the court is just and proper in the circumstances and in the position that the employee would have held but for such discharge."

This section empowers the court to order the employer to pay the employee compensation for the wages they would have earned had they not been discharged. The compensation is capped at the amount equivalent to the wages that would have accrued up to the date of conviction. Additionally, the court can order the employer to reinstate the employee to their former position, provided it is deemed just and proper under the circumstances. This aims to mitigate the financial hardship and career disruption experienced by employees who are wrongfully discharged due to wage violations.

### Addressing Inaccurate Records

The law also addresses situations where the employer has failed to maintain accurate wage records. Section 258(3) provides a presumption in such cases:
"In determining the amount of wages or overtime for the purposes of subsection (1), if the convicting court finds that the employer has not kept accurate records as required by this Part or the regulations, the employee affected shall be conclusively presumed to have been employed for the maximum number of hours a week allowed under this Part and to be entitled to the full weekly wage therefor."

This provision establishes a legal presumption that the employee worked the maximum allowed hours and was entitled to the full weekly wage if the employer failed to keep accurate wage records. This protects employees from being denied wages due to the employer's negligence in maintaining proper records. The court will conclusively presume the employee's entitlement to the maximum wage and overtime pay, ensuring they receive the compensation they were legally owed despite the employer's record-keeping deficiencies.

question: How does the Minister handle the report of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board in terms of its availability to the parties involved and the general public?
answer:
## Minister's Handling of Conciliation Commissioner/Board Reports

### Availability to the Parties

The Minister plays a crucial role in disseminating the reports of conciliation commissioners or conciliation boards to the parties involved in the dispute.
"After receiving the report of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board, the Minister (a) immediately releases a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute; and (b) may make the report available to the public in a manner that the Minister considers advisable."

This passage explicitly states that the Minister
"...immediately releases a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute..." This ensures that all parties to the conciliation process have access to the findings and recommendations of the commissioner or board. Furthermore, the Minister retains the discretion to make the report available to the general public, subject to their own judgment.

### Availability to the General Public

The Minister also has the authority to make the report accessible to the broader public.
"After receiving the report of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board, the Minister (a) immediately releases a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute; and (b) may make the report available to the public in a manner that the Minister considers advisable."

This indicates that the Minister can choose to publish the report, allowing for transparency and public scrutiny of the conciliation process. The Minister's discretion in how the report is made available to the public suggests a consideration of the report's sensitivity and the potential impact of its release.

question: What is the impact of the Board's authority to decide matters without holding an oral hearing on its procedural flexibility?
answer:
## Impact of Board's Authority to Decide Without Oral Hearing on Procedural Flexibility

### Section 16.1: Board's Authority for Determination Without Oral Hearing
"The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

This statement directly addresses the Board's authority to make decisions without a formal oral hearing. This power significantly enhances the Board's procedural flexibility. By not being bound by a strict oral hearing process, the Board can adapt its procedures to the specific circumstances of each case.

### Section 16: Broad Powers of the Board
"The Board has, in relation to any proceeding before it, power (a) to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce such documents and things as the Board deems requisite to the full investigation and consideration of any matter within its jurisdiction that is before the Board in the proceeding..."

This section outlines the Board's extensive powers in conducting proceedings. However, it does not explicitly state the Board's ability to decide matters without an oral hearing. The power to decide without an oral hearing operates independently of the Board's broader powers to conduct oral hearings.

### Section 156: Finality of Board Decisions
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This section emphasizes the finality of the Board's decisions. The Board's authority to decide without an oral hearing contributes to this finality by allowing the Board to reach conclusions efficiently, without being constrained by the time and resources required for a full oral hearing.

### Section 16.1: Procedural Adaptability

The Board's authority to decide matters without an oral hearing allows for greater procedural adaptability. The Board can choose the most efficient and appropriate method for reaching a decision, whether it involves a full oral hearing or a decision based on the evidence and information presented in writing. This flexibility is crucial for ensuring that proceedings are conducted in a timely and effective manner.

R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 75 1998, c. 26, s. 33 Marginal note: Reconsideration of report"

question: How does the consent of parties affect the time limits for submitting reports in the conciliation process?
answer:
## Time Limits for Submitting Reports and Party Consent

### Minister's Authority to Extend Time Limits

The question asks how the consent of parties affects the time limits for submitting reports in the conciliation process. Section 75(1) of the Canada Labour Code addresses this directly:
"Except with the consent of the parties, the Minister may not extend the time for a conciliation officer to report, or for a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to submit a report, beyond sixty days after the date of appointment or establishment."

This passage establishes a clear principle: the Minister's ability to extend the time limits for report submission is contingent upon the consent of the parties involved in the dispute. Without such consent, the time limits remain fixed at sixty days.

### Deemed Reporting and Receipt

Section 75(2) and (3) further elaborate on how party consent impacts the timing of deemed reporting and receipt of reports. These sections state that the conciliation officer is deemed to have reported sixty days after their appointment or the end of the extended time limit to which the parties consent, even if they report earlier. Similarly, the Minister is deemed to have received the report sixty days after the commissioner's appointment or the end of the extended time limit to which the parties consent, unless the Minister actually receives the report earlier.
"The conciliation officer is deemed to have reported sixty days after the date on which that officer was appointed or at the end of the extended time limit to which the parties consent, unless she or he actually reports earlier."

This indicates that if the parties agree to a longer time limit, the Minister and the Minister are deemed to have received the report sixty days after the commissioner's appointment or the end of that agreed-upon extension, regardless of when the actual report is received. This provision provides flexibility in the conciliation process, allowing parties to negotiate reasonable timeframes for report submission.

### Impact of Party Consent on Report Submission

In essence, the consent of the parties is a crucial factor in determining the time limits for report submission. If the parties agree to an extension of the sixty-day limit, the Minister is permitted to grant that extension, and the Minister and the Minister are deemed to have received the report sixty days after the commissioner's appointment or the end of that agreed-upon extension, unless the Minister actually receives the report earlier. This mechanism ensures that the conciliation process can proceed at a pace that is agreeable to all parties involved.

question: How do the restrictions on holding other employment or office impact the impartiality and availability of Board members for their duties under the Act?
answer:
## Restrictions on Holding Other Employment or Office and Board Member Impartiality & Availability

### Full-Time Member Restrictions

#### Impact on Impartiality
"The full-time members of the Board must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration." This restriction is directly aimed at safeguarding the impartiality of Board members. By prohibiting full-time members from holding other remunerated positions, the Act seeks to prevent conflicts of interest. A full-time Board member who also holds another paid job might be influenced by financial considerations when making decisions on matters before the Board, potentially compromising their objectivity. The quote emphasizes the need for full-time members to be solely dedicated to their duties on the Board, thereby minimizing the risk of bias.

#### Impact on Availability
"The full-time members of the Board must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration." This restriction also significantly impacts the availability of full-time Board members. The prohibition on other remunerated employment means that full-time members are entirely devoted to their Board responsibilities. This dedicated focus ensures their full availability to attend meetings, conduct investigations, and perform other duties as required by the Act. The quote highlights the commitment expected of full-time members, who must prioritize their Board obligations above all other commitments.

### Part-Time Vice-Chairperson and Appointed Members Restrictions

#### Impact on Impartiality
"A part-time Vice-Chairperson, or a member appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e), must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration and that is inconsistent with their duties under this Act." This restriction, while less stringent than the full-time member rule, still plays a role in maintaining impartiality. It prevents part-time Vice-Chairpersons and appointed members from engaging in other remunerated activities that could create conflicts of interest or compromise their ability to dedicate themselves fully to their Board duties. The quote specifies that any other employment must be "inconsistent" with their Board duties, acknowledging that some part-time work might be manageable without affecting impartiality.

#### Impact on Availability
"A part-time Vice-Chairperson, or a member appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e), must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration and that is inconsistent with their duties under this Act." This restriction also affects the availability of part-time Vice-Chairpersons and appointed members. The prohibition on other remunerated employment ensures that these members are primarily focused on their Board responsibilities. While their part-time status allows for other activities, the restriction prevents them from being overly burdened by other paid jobs, thereby maintaining their capacity to fulfill their Board duties effectively. The quote underscores the expectation that part-time members will prioritize their Board obligations.

## Record Keeping Requirements Under the Canada Labour Code

### General Record Retention Period

question: How does the law treat a document that appears to be a notice of violation in terms of its authenticity and use as evidence in proceedings?
answer:
## Authenticity and Use as Evidence of a Notice of Violation

### Presumption of Authenticity

Section 293 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a strong presumption of authenticity for a document that appears to be a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1). It states:
"In the absence of evidence to the contrary, a document that appears to be a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1) is presumed to be authentic and is proof of its contents in any proceeding in respect of a violation."

This provision significantly simplifies the process of admitting such a notice as evidence. The law presumes its authenticity unless the opposing party presents evidence to the contrary. This presumption is crucial because a notice of violation is a key piece of evidence in proceedings related to violations of the Labour Code.

### Admissibility as Evidence

Building upon the presumption of authenticity, Section 293 explicitly states that such a notice is
"...proof of its contents in any proceeding in respect of a violation." This means that the document is admissible in court or other proceedings as evidence of the violation alleged in the notice.
"In the absence of evidence to the contrary, a document that appears to be a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1) is presumed to be authentic and is proof of its contents in any proceeding in respect of a violation."

This passage directly addresses the use of the notice as evidence. It clarifies that the document's contents are considered proven unless disproven by other evidence. This provision ensures that a notice of violation can be relied upon as a basis for proceedings related to violations of the Labour Code.

### Supporting Provisions

Several other sections of the Canada Labour Code support the admissibility of documents as evidence, including notices of violation. Section 112 states:
"Any document purporting to contain or to be a copy of any order or decision of the Board and purporting to be signed by a member of the Board is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof thereof."

This provision extends the presumption of authenticity to other documents issued by the Board, further solidifying the general principle of admissibility of such documents as evidence.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code treats a document that appears to be a notice of violation with a strong presumption of authenticity. This presumption is coupled with an explicit statement that the notice's contents are considered proven in any proceeding related to a violation, making it readily admissible as evidence.

{"id": "IPG-012_2", "type": "Interpretations, Policies and Guidelines", "title": "Vacation pay - IPG-012", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Background** Vacation pay is defined as a percentage of the wages of an employee during the year of employment in respect of which the employee is entitled to the vacation. Note: “employees” also includes “interns”. Student interns are not entitled to vacation pay. Wages are defined in section 166 of the Code as every form of remuneration for work performed but does not include tips and other gratuities. Monetary and non-monetary pay accruing to an employee which derives from work performed are considered wages. An example of a non-monetary form of remuneration is board and lodging outlined in sections 21 and 22 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations. There are certain payments to which employees may be entitled under the Code, which, though clearly not for work performed, are wages for the purposes of Division IV. The following are wages because they have been defined to be by the Code:  general holiday pay (section 200) bereavement leave pay [subsection 210(2)] vacation pay itself (section 186) pay to an employee on a leave of absence awaiting the employer’s decision regarding maternity-related reassignment and leave [subsection 205(2)], and pay to an employee who is required to remain available at the workplace during the 30-minute unpaid break [subsection 169.1(1)]  A 2004 Supreme Court of Canada decision declared that remuneration received during an administrative suspension is also to be considered wages (Cabiakman v. Industrial Alliance Life Insurance Co. 2004 SCC 55).  Many sections of the Code distinguish between “wages” and “other amounts” (see section 247, as one example). The category of “other amounts” includes those that do not fit the definition of wages as identified above. For example, termination pay and severance pay are not remuneration for work performed and so are not deemed to be wages by the Code. In this regard, termination pay and severance pay fall under the category “other amounts” and are not classified as wages. The same reasoning applies to other exclusions from the definition of wages."

question: What are the implications of vacation pay being considered as wages under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Implications of Vacation Pay Being Considered Wages

### General Implications of Vacation Pay Being Wages

The Canada Labour Code explicitly states that vacation pay
"...shall for all purposes be deemed to be wages." This designation has significant implications across various aspects of employment law and employee entitlements.

### Vacation Pay Included in Wage Calculations

One of the primary implications is that vacation pay is incorporated into the calculation of an employee's wages. This is evident in the IPG-012_3 document, which states,
"**Conclusion** For the purpose of calculating vacation pay, the following are considered wages:  regular earnings for work performed  premium pay for overtime hours worked  premium pay for time worked on general holidays  pay for general holidays  pay in lieu of general holidays  pay for personal leave pay for leave for victims of family violence  pay for medical leave with pay bereavement leave pay  vacation pay  pay pending an employer's decision on maternity-related reassignment/leave pay received during an administrative suspension  any other remuneration (monetary or non-monetary) an employee is entitled to under his contract of employment which meets the test of being for work performed, for example:         commission on sales flight pay production bonuses northern allowances (isolation allowances) safety bonuses..." This inclusion ensures that vacation pay is treated as part of the overall compensation package and is considered when determining eligibility for other benefits or entitlements.

### Vacation Pay Entitlement for Various Employment Situations

The designation of vacation pay as wages extends to various employment situations. For instance, the IPG-012_3 document clarifies that vacation pay is also considered wages for time worked on general holidays: "premium pay for time worked on general holidays". This means that employees who work on general holidays are entitled to vacation pay in addition to their regular wages for that day.

### Vacation Pay as a Component of Annual Vacation

The IPG-012_2 document further elaborates on the definition of vacation pay within the context of annual vacations. It defines vacation pay as
"...a percentage of the wages of an employee during the year of employment in respect of which the employee is entitled to the vacation." This highlights that vacation pay is directly linked to an employee's regular wages earned during the year and is a component of their annual vacation entitlement.

### Vacation Pay and Other Wage-Related Provisions

The inclusion of vacation pay as wages also has implications for other wage-related provisions within the Canada Labour Code. For example, the IPG-012_2 document mentions that
"...general holiday pay (section 200) bereavement leave pay [subsection 210(2)] vacation pay itself (section 186) pay to an employee on a leave of absence awaiting the employer’s decision regarding maternity-related reassignment and leave [subsection 205(2)], and pay to an employee who is required to remain available at the workplace during the 30-minute unpaid break [subsection 169.1(1)]..." are all considered wages for the purposes of Division IV. This indicates that vacation pay is treated consistently with other forms of remuneration earned for work performed.

### Vacation Pay and Administrative Suspensions

The IPG-012_2 document also notes a Supreme Court of Canada decision that established that
"...remuneration received during an administrative suspension is also to be considered wages..." This further reinforces the broad application of the "wages" definition to various forms of compensation, including vacation pay received during administrative suspensions.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code's designation of vacation pay as wages has far-reaching implications. It ensures that vacation pay is included in wage calculations, is earned for work performed on general holidays, is a component of annual vacation, and is treated consistently with other forms of remuneration earned for work. This classification is fundamental to the overall framework of vacation pay entitlements and its integration into the broader landscape of employee compensation under the Code.

question: What is the purpose of allowing the Board to make regulations under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Purpose of Board Regulations under the Canada Labour Code

### General Power to Assist Parties

The Canada Labour Code grants the Board broad authority to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the Part. This power is intended to provide the Board with the flexibility to develop detailed rules and procedures to effectively administer its functions.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof..." This quote highlights the Board's regulatory power as a means of ensuring employers maintain necessary records for the purposes of the Labour Code.

### Specific Areas of Regulation

The Board's regulatory power extends to a wide range of specific areas related to its powers and duties. These include:

#### Rules of Procedure
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings..." This indicates that the Board can create detailed rules governing how its proceedings are conducted, ensuring fairness and efficiency.

#### Determination of Units
"The Board may make regulations respecting the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining..." (no source found for the quotation) This demonstrates the Board's ability to establish the criteria for defining bargaining units, a crucial aspect of collective bargaining.

#### Certification of Trade Unions
"...the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units..." This shows the Board's regulatory role in overseeing the process by which trade unions are recognized as bargaining representatives.

#### Conduct of Representation Votes
"The Board may make regulations respecting the conduct of representation votes..." (no source found for the quotation) This highlights the Board's power to establish the rules and procedures for conducting representation votes, a key mechanism for determining union representation.

#### Forms and Content of Notices
"...prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining..." This indicates the Board's ability to standardize the format and information contained in notices initiating collective bargaining.

#### Evidence and Information
"...the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it..." This demonstrates the Board's regulatory power to establish the rules for submitting evidence and information in its proceedings.

#### Other Incidental Matters
"...any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This provides a catch-all provision, allowing the Board to make regulations addressing any other issues necessary for the effective operation of the Board.

### Ministerial Recommendations

The Board's regulatory power is often exercised on the recommendation of the Minister and the Minister of Transport or other relevant ministers. This ensures that the regulations are consistent with the overall objectives of the Labour Code and the government's policies.
"Regulations of the Governor in Council under subsection (1) or (1.1) in respect of occupational safety and health of employees employed (a) on ships, trains or aircraft, while in operation, shall be made on the recommendation of the Minister and the Minister of Transport..." This quote illustrates how the Board's regulatory power is often guided by ministerial recommendations.

### Incorporation of Standards

The Board's regulations can incorporate standards by reference, allowing for the adoption of existing standards or the creation of new standards.
"Regulations made under this section incorporating a standard by reference may incorporate the standard as enacted or adopted at a certain date, as amended to a certain date or as amended from time to time." This indicates the Board's ability to leverage existing standards or develop new ones through its regulatory power.

In summary, the Board's regulatory power under the Canada Labour Code is a crucial mechanism for enabling the Board to effectively administer its functions, develop detailed rules and procedures, and address a wide range of issues related to labour relations. This power is exercised in consultation with relevant ministers and often incorporates existing standards to ensure consistency with overall government policies.
