question: What is the general purpose of the provisions related to leaves of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Purpose of Leaves of Absence Provisions

### Entitlement to Leave for Reserve Force Members

The primary purpose of the provisions related to leaves of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code is to grant certain employees who are members of the reserve force the right to take leaves of absence for specific military operations, activities, and training. This ensures that reserve force members can fulfill their duties while still maintaining their employment.
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..."

This section clearly establishes the entitlement to leave for reserve force members, outlining the minimum continuous employment requirement and the types of operations and activities for which leave can be granted.

### Entitlement to Leave for Other Military and Civil Duties

Beyond reserve force operations, the provisions also extend leave entitlements to employees called out on service for various military and civil duties.
"(d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This passage details the various military and civil duties for which leave can be granted, including training, duties performed on active service, service in aid of civil power, and treatment for health problems resulting from service.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

While the provisions grant leave entitlements, they also include a maximum duration to prevent excessive disruptions to employment.
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period."

This limitation ensures that reserve force members and employees called out on service do not take leaves that are unduly long and cause significant hardship to their employers.

### Exceptions to Leave Entitlement

The provisions also specify certain exceptions to the leave entitlement.
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave."

This exception allows the Head of the National Defence to deny a leave request if it would negatively impact public health or safety or create undue hardship for the employer.

### Regulations for Implementation

The provisions also authorize the Governor in Council to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Division.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Division and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) specifying the absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment for the purpose of subsection 247.5(1); (b) specifying what constitutes or does not constitute an operation for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(a); (c) setting out the activities for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(b); (d) defining “military skills training” for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(c); (e) limiting the duration of the treatment, recovery or rehabilitation referred to in paragraph 247.5(1)(g) or setting out the terms or conditions for the application of that paragraph; (f) specifying what constitutes or does not constitute undue hardship for the purposes of subsection 247.5(4); (g) specifying what constitutes or does not constitute a valid reason for the purposes of subsection 247.6(1), (2), (3) or (4), 247.7(3) or 247.93(2); (h) specifying the circumstances in which section 247.7, subsection 247.8(1) or subsection 247.91(2) does not apply; (i) specifying the circumstances in which an employer may not assign an employee to a position with different terms or conditions of employment for the purposes of section 247.94; (j) [Repealed, 2018, c. 27, s. 495] (k) [Repealed, 2018, c. 27, s. 495] (l) prescribing the classes of employees that are not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if the Governor in Council is satisfied that the fact of taking leave would cause unreasonable consequences..."

This section grants broad authority to the Governor in Council to create detailed rules and procedures for implementing the leave entitlements, addressing various aspects such as defining operations, specifying activities, and outlining exceptions.

In summary, the general purpose of the provisions related to leaves of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code is to provide a framework for granting employees who are members of the reserve force and those called out on service the right to take leaves for specific military and civil duties, while also setting limits on the duration of such leaves and providing for certain exceptions. The regulations made by the Governor in Council further elaborate on the implementation of these leave entitlements.

question: What are the conditions under which a person can file a payment order or a Board order in the Federal Court, and are there any circumstances that prevent such filing?
answer:
## Conditions for Filing Payment Orders or Board Orders in Federal Court

### General Conditions for Filing

Section 251.15 outlines the general conditions for filing a payment order or a Board order in the Federal Court. It states:
"Any person who is affected by a payment order issued under subsection 251.1(1) or confirmed or varied under subsection 251.101(3) or by an order of the Board made under subsection 251.12(1), or the Head, may, after the day provided in the order for compliance or after 15 days following the day on which the order is issued, made, confirmed or varied, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the payment order, or a copy of the order of the Board, exclusive of reasons."

This indicates that any individual or entity impacted by a payment order or a Board order has the right to file a copy of that order in the Federal Court. The timeframe for filing is specified as either the date provided in the order for compliance or 15 days after the order is issued, whichever is later.

### Circumstances Preventing Filing

Section 251.15 also details specific circumstances that prevent the filing of a payment order or a Board order in the Federal Court. It states:
"However, a payment order is not to be filed while it is or may be the subject of a review under subsection 251.101(1) or an appeal under subsection 251.101(7) or section 251.11 or if an order of the Board is made under paragraph 251.12(1)(a) relating to the payment order."

This passage clearly identifies situations where filing a payment order or a Board order is prohibited. Specifically, it prohibits filing while the order is or may be under review or appeal, or if a Board order is made concerning the payment order itself.

### Enforcement of Orders

Section 251.15 further explains the process of enforcement of orders filed in the Federal Court. It states:
"On the filing of a copy of an order in the Federal Court under subsection (1) or (2), the order shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

This indicates that once a payment order or a Board order is filed in the Federal Court, it is registered and gains the same legal force as a judgment obtained in that Court. This allows for the enforcement of the order through the Federal Court system.

### Filing in Provincial Superior Court

Section 23.1 provides an alternative option for filing a payment order or a Board order, which is in the superior court of a province. It states:
"The Board may, on application by a person or organization affected by an order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the superior court of a province."

This passage clarifies that the Board has the authority to file a copy of an order in the superior court of a province upon request from an affected party. It also notes that Section 23 applies to such a superior court filing, with any necessary modifications.

question: What actions can the Board take if a trade union or employers' organization fails to provide its members with a financial statement as required?
answer:
## Board Actions for Failure to Provide Financial Statements

### Board Order for Filing Statement
"The Board, on the complaint of any member of a trade union or employers’ organization that it has failed to comply with subsection (1), may make an order requiring the trade union or employers’ organization to file with the Board, within the time set out in the order, a statement in such form and with such particulars as the Board may determine."

This section outlines the Board's power to issue an order compelling a trade union or employers' organization to submit a financial statement. The Board can act upon a member's complaint about a failure to provide the statement. The order will specify the required format and level of detail for the statement. This demonstrates the Board's ability to enforce the financial disclosure requirement.

### Board Order for Providing Statement to Members
"The Board may make an order requiring a trade union or employers’ organization to provide a copy of a statement filed under subsection (3) to such members of the trade union or employers’ organization as the Board in its discretion directs."

This subsection further elaborates on the Board's enforcement mechanisms. The Board can order a trade union or employers' organization to furnish a copy of a filed financial statement to its members. The Board retains discretion over which members receive the statement. This action ensures that members have access to the financial information of their organization, even if the organization initially fails to provide it directly.

### Complaint to Board for Failure to Provide Financial Statement
"The Board, on the complaint of any member of a trade union or employers’ organization that it has failed to comply with subsection (1), may make an order requiring the trade union or employers’ organization to file with the Board, within the time set out in the order, a statement in such form and with such particulars as the Board may determine."

This point reiterates the Board's ability to respond to a member's complaint about a failure to provide financial statements. The Board can then issue an order requiring the organization to file the statement with the Board within a specified timeframe and format. This action underscores the Board's role in ensuring compliance with the financial disclosure requirement by addressing individual member concerns.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-25_7", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Collective voice for non-unionized workers: Issue paper", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Declining unionization** Interest in mechanisms for collective voice has been spurred by the steady decline in unionization in Canada and across the industrialized world over the past half-century. According to Statistics Canada data,Footnote 7 the proportion of employees in the Canadian workforce who are not unionized rose from 62% in 1981 to 70% in 2017, with most of the increase taking place in the late 1980s and throughout the 1990s and amongst male workers and young workers. The non-unionization rate for women remained very stable over the period, hovering between 68% and 71%. Why the overall decline in unionization has occurred has sparked considerable research interest. One important factor has clearly been structural changes in the Canadian economy and the labour force, such as the reduction in the share of employment accounted for by more highly unionized industries (for example, manufacturing and mining) and in the share of blue-collar occupations within industries. Another is globalization, at least in manufacturing, which has increased the credibility of employer threats of job loss in the event of employees unionizing. Research also shows that the adoption of mandatory vote systems for union certification, as has occurred in some jurisdictions in Canada beginning with Nova Scotia in 1977, British Columbia in 1984 and Alberta in 1988, is associated with reductions in unionization rates (Riddell, 2004). However, it is not clear whether that is because mandatory vote systems allow employees to voice their preference more freely compared to card-check systems, or because employers are more able to interfere in employees’ choices. Relatedly, employer resistance to unionization or use of suppression practices, such as interfering in certification drives, purposefully disrupting work schedules to make it more difficult for employees to participate in union activities and communicating anti-union sentiments, can impact unionization rates. In a 2002 study of eight Canadian jurisdictions, Bentham found that employer resistance to certification applications was the norm, with 80% of employers overtly and actively opposing union certification drives. She also concluded that, depending on its form, employer resistance can have an impact on both initial certification outcomes and on the probability that the parties will establish and sustain a positive collective bargaining relationship. She notes, however, that a handful of researchers have concluded that employer interference, such as shifting work to other facilities, “may, in some instances, cause a rebound effect and increase, as opposed to undermine, worker solidarity.” Other studies have found that many workers today simply do not want to join a union. When asked in a 2013 Harris/Decima poll conducted for the Canadian Association of University Teachers, 43% of the 2,000 Canadians who responded agreed with the statement “If I had a choice, I’d never join a union” and 45% disagreed (CAUT Council, 2013). One of the key reasons why people hold negative views towards unions is that they see them as large, remote, bureaucratic organizations that foster adversarial rather than cooperative solutions (Gomez, 2016). Union wage stagnation and the erosion of certain benefits may also reduce the appeal of unionization. Accounting for differences in occupation, education and age between unionized and non-unionized workers, the union wage premium between workers—the difference in wages between union and non-union workers—has been falling steadily in Canada, from about 20% in the 1980s to 8% in 2002 (Fang and Verma, 2002). In addition, wage increases settled through bargaining have barely exceeded inflation in recent years, in both the public and private sectors (Jackson, 2013). Another key theme in the literature is the failure of unions themselves to respond to the “representation gap”, or unsatisfied demand for union membership. About one in three non-unionized workers in Canada consistently say that they would like to join a union if they had the opportunity (Gomez, 2016). The representation gap has been a common factor in calls for union renewal through “organizing the unorganized”, greater union democracy and other strategies, especially since the 2000s (Kumar, 2008; Rose, 2008). On the other hand, the desire for alternative, non-union models of collective representation is high. Gomez (2016) has estimated, using 2014 data, that 73% of Canadian workers are either definitely or probably willing to participate in an employee organization other than a traditional union that discusses workplace issues with management (compared to just under 40% who would prefer to belong to a union). In addition, there are reasons to believe that support for non-union mechanisms for collective voice is higher amongst some groups, such as millennial workers who now make up the largest cohort in the Canadian workforce, have high expectations about being engaged in the workplace and are more likely to opt for “exit” when they are unhappy in the workplace (Hawkins et al., 2014)."

question: Can an employer's actions during a unionization effort influence the Board's decision to certify a trade union, even if the union doesn't have majority support?
answer:
## Employer Actions and Board Certification Despite Lack of Majority Support

### Section 25 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 25 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the influence of employer actions on the Board's certification decision, even when a union lacks majority support. It states:
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for any unit comprised of employees of the employer and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer that applies to any such employees shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part."

This section is crucial because it explicitly permits the Board to deny certification even if a union has majority support if the employer has exerted such a dominant influence that the union's ability to represent employees is compromised. The Board's assessment of employer influence is a key factor, regardless of the union's current membership.

### Section 29 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 29 further elaborates on the Board's ability to order a representation vote when employer actions are suspected. It mentions:
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This passage highlights that employer actions, such as actively opposing union certification drives, can lead the Board to order a representation vote to gauge the employees' true preference. The Board's satisfaction that the union has at least 35% membership is a threshold, but employer interference can trigger this vote even if the union falls short of majority support.

### Section 30 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 30 details the Board's procedures for conducting a representation vote, implicitly acknowledging the potential influence of employer actions. It states:
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

This section emphasizes the Board's role in ensuring a fair representation vote, which is often necessary when employer actions cast doubt on the union's true support. The Board's ability to make arrangements for the vote is a mechanism to address potential employer interference.

### Labour Reports - 25_7

The Labour Reports document provides broader context on employer resistance to unionization and its impact on certification outcomes. It notes:
"She also concluded that, depending on its form, employer resistance can have an impact on both initial certification outcomes and on the probability that the parties will establish and sustain a positive collective bargaining relationship. She notes, however, that a handful of researchers have concluded that employer interference, such as shifting work to other facilities, “may, in some instances, cause a rebound effect and increase, as opposed to undermine, worker solidarity.”..."

This passage directly addresses the influence of employer actions. It states that employer resistance, including interference like shifting work, can affect certification outcomes. Furthermore, it suggests that such interference might even strengthen worker solidarity in some cases. This indicates that employer actions are a significant factor the Board considers when deciding whether to certify a union, even if it lacks majority support.

In conclusion, an employer's actions during a unionization effort can significantly influence the Board's decision to certify a trade union, even if the union doesn't have majority support. The Board is empowered to deny certification if the employer has exerted such a dominant influence that the union's ability to represent employees is impaired. Employer resistance to unionization, including interference in certification drives, can also trigger a representation vote to determine the employees' true preference.

question: Can an employer refuse an employee who is a member of the reserve force a leave of absence, and if so, under what conditions?
answer:
## Employer Refusal of Reserve Force Leave of Absence

### General Prohibition

The Canada Labour Code explicitly prohibits employers from refusing an employee a leave of absence for reserve force duties under Division XV.2. Section 247.96 states:
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them."

This provision establishes a clear legal protection for reserve force members seeking leave. It prohibits any adverse employment action taken against an employee solely because of their reserve force membership or their intention to take leave.

### Conditions for Refusal

However, the law does outline specific conditions under which an employer *may* refuse a leave of absence. Section 247.5(4) states:
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..."

This indicates that an employer may refuse a leave of absence if it would cause undue hardship to the employer or adversely affect public health or safety. Section 247.5(4) elaborates on this:
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..."

This means that an employer may refuse a leave of absence if it would cause undue hardship to the employer or adversely affect public health or safety.

### Notice Requirements

If an employer intends to refuse a leave of absence due to undue hardship, they must provide the employee with a notice. Section 247.95(2) states:
"The employer of an employee who is on leave and whose wages or benefits would be changed as a result of the reorganization shall, as soon as practicable, send a notice to the employee at their last known address."

This notice must explain the reason for the refusal and the potential consequences.

### Request for Proof

An employer may request proof that a leave of absence is taken under this Division. Section 247.7(1) states:
"Subject to subsection (2), if the employer requests proof that a leave of absence is taken under this Division, the employee shall provide the employer with the prescribed document, if any, or with a document that is approved by the Chief of the Defence Staff who was appointed under subsection 18(1) of the National Defence Act..."

This request for proof is subject to certain conditions, as outlined in subsection (2).

### Return to Work Postponement

If an employee does not notify the employer at least four weeks before the day on which the leave that is taken under this Division is to end, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the end date of the leave. Section 247.8(1) states:
"If the employee does not notify the employer at least four weeks before the day on which the leave that is taken under this Division is to end, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the end date of the leave."

This postponement is deemed to be part of the leave.

R.S., c. L-1, s. 130 1972, c. 18, s. 1 1977-78, c. 27, s. 48 Marginal note: Designation of employers’ organization"

question: How can a council of trade unions become certified as a bargaining agent for a unit under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Certification of a Council of Trade Unions as a Bargaining Agent

### Application to the Board
"Where two or more trade unions have formed a council of trade unions, the council so formed may apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in the same manner as a trade union." This section directly addresses the process for a council of trade unions to achieve certification. It establishes that a council can make an application to the Board for certification using the same procedure as an individual trade union. This indicates that the requirements for individual trade union certification apply equally to councils formed by multiple unions.

### Board Satisfaction with Requirements
"The Board may certify a council of trade unions as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit where the Board is satisfied that the requirements for certification prescribed by or pursuant to this Part have been met." This passage elaborates on the Board's role in the certification process for councils. It states that the Board's decision to certify a council hinges on its satisfaction that the council has fulfilled all the criteria outlined in the Canada Labour Code for trade union certification. This implies that the Board will assess the council's membership, the wishes of the employees in the bargaining unit, and other relevant factors to determine if the council meets the certification standards.

### Membership in the Council
"Membership in any trade union that forms part of a council of trade unions is deemed to be membership in the council of trade unions." This clarifies the concept of membership within a council. It states that if a trade union is a part of a council, then its members are also considered members of the council. This is important because it ensures that the council's representation is based on the collective membership of its constituent unions.

### Council's Binding Agreement
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union." This section outlines the legal implications of a council's certification. It specifies that the council, along with each of its constituent unions, is legally bound by any collective agreement it enters into with the employer. Furthermore, it states that the rest of the Canada Labour Code applies to the council as if it were a single trade union, providing a consistent framework for collective bargaining.

R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 120 2003, c. 22, s. 224(E)"

question: Under what circumstances can the Government of Canada administer legislation enacted by a provincial legislature?
answer:
## Arrangements with Provinces: Where Uniform Provincial Legislation

### Section 120(1)
"Where this Part and legislation enacted by the legislature of a province are substantially uniform, the Minister may, on behalf of the Government of Canada, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with the government of the province to provide for the administration of the legislation of the province by officers and employees employed in the federal public administration."

This section outlines the primary circumstance under which the Government of Canada can administer legislation enacted by a provincial legislature. It states that when federal and provincial legislation are "substantially uniform," the Minister, with the Governor in Council's approval, can enter into an agreement with the provincial government. This agreement would allow federal public administration officers and employees to handle the administration of the provincial legislation. The rationale behind this provision is to streamline governance where the legal frameworks are largely aligned, avoiding duplication of administrative efforts.

### Section 120(2)
"An agreement made pursuant to subsection (1) in respect of the administration of any legislation of a province may provide (a) for the administration by Canada of the legislation of the province with respect to any particular work, undertaking or business; (b) that the Minister may, on behalf of the province, exercise the powers conferred or perform the duties imposed under the legislation of the province; (c) that the members of the Board, or officers and employees employed in the federal public administration, may exercise the powers conferred or perform the duties imposed under the legislation of the province; and (d) for payment by the government of the province to the Government of Canada for expenses incurred by the Government of Canada in the administration of the legislation of the province."

This subsection elaborates on the potential content of such an agreement. It details various ways in which the Government of Canada could administer provincial legislation. One possibility is for Canada to directly administer the legislation with respect to specific areas. Another is for the Minister to act on behalf of the province, exercising the powers and fulfilling the duties outlined in the provincial legislation. Furthermore, it allows for the involvement of Board members or federal public administration officers in carrying out these administrative tasks. Finally, it addresses the financial aspect, stating that the provincial government would compensate the federal government for any expenses incurred in administering the provincial legislation.

### Section 120(3)
"Where an agreement has been entered into between the Government of Canada and the government of a province in respect of any legislation of the province, the Minister, the members of the Board and any officers or employees employed in the federal public administration may, if the legislation so provides and the Governor in Council so orders, exercise the powers and perform the duties specified in the legislation or agreement."

This final subsection clarifies the operational aspect of the agreement. It states that once an agreement is in place, various federal officials – the Minister, Board members, and federal public administration officers – are authorized to exercise the powers and perform the duties specified in the provincial legislation or the agreement itself. This provision ensures that the federal government has the necessary authority to carry out the administrative functions delegated to it under the intergovernmental agreement.

question: What are the implications for an employer who is granted a permit to have employees work beyond the maximum hours of work specified in the Canada Labour Code, and what reporting requirements must they fulfill?
answer:
## Implications for an Employer Granted an Excess Hours Permit

### Authorization and Conditions
"On the application of an employer or an employer’s organization, the Head, having regard to the conditions of employment in any industrial establishment and the welfare of the employees, may, by a permit in writing, authorize hours to be worked by any class of employees set out in the permit in excess of the maximum hours of work specified in or prescribed under section 171, established under section 172 or prescribed by regulations made under section 175." This section outlines the process for obtaining an excess hours permit. An employer must apply to the Head, who will then decide whether to grant the permit based on the specific circumstances of the workplace and the well-being of the employees. The permit specifies the number of additional hours employees may work.

### Justification and Notice Requirements
"No permit may be issued under subsection (1) unless the applicant has satisfied the Head (a) that exceptional circumstances exist that justify the working of additional hours; (b) that the employer had posted a notice of the application for the permit, for at least 30 days before its proposed effective date, in places readily accessible to the affected class of employees where they were likely to see it; and (c) that the employer had informed the trade union in writing of the application for the permit, if those employees are represented by a trade union." This subsection details the conditions that must be met for a permit to be issued. The employer must demonstrate that the extra work is due to exceptional circumstances, provide adequate notice of the application to affected employees and any relevant trade unions, and justify the need for the additional hours.

### Duration and Additional Hour Specification
"A permit under subsection (1) shall be issued for the period specified therein, which shall not be longer than the period during which it is anticipated that the exceptional circumstances that justified the permit will continue." This clarifies that the permit has a limited duration, tied to the expected length of the exceptional circumstances necessitating the extra hours.
"A permit under subsection (1) may specify either (a) the total of the number of additional hours in excess of the maximum hours specified in or prescribed under section 171 or by regulations made under section 175, or (b) the additional hours that may be worked in any day and in any week during the period of the permit." This indicates that the permit can either specify the total number of extra hours allowed or the maximum number of extra hours that can be worked per day or week during the permit's validity.

### Reporting Requirements
"If a permit has been issued under this section, the employer for whom or on whose behalf the permit was issued shall report in writing to the Head, within 15 days after the expiration of the period specified in the permit or within such time as the Head may fix in the permit, stating the number of employees who worked in excess of the maximum hours specified in or prescribed under section 171 or by regulations made under section 175 and the number of additional hours each of them worked." This section outlines the mandatory reporting requirements for employers who receive an excess hours permit. The employer must submit a written report to the Head within 15 days after the permit expires, detailing the number of employees who worked beyond the maximum hours and the number of additional hours each of them worked.

## Additional Implications
"Obtaining a permit does not exempt the employer from the obligation to pay overtime. The employer must report in writing to the Head within 15 days after the permit expires or at another date specified in the permit. The report must show the number of:  employees who worked more than 48 hours in a week, and additional hours in a week each employee worked..." This further clarifies that while a permit allows for exceeding the maximum hours, employers are still obligated to pay overtime for hours worked beyond 48 in a week. The report submitted to the Head must also include this overtime information.

question: What are the requirements for reporting and documenting the findings of an investigation or inquiry into a workplace incident, including the timeframe for providing the report to relevant parties?
answer:
## Workplace Incident Investigation and Reporting Requirements

### Accident Investigations and Reporting

#### Serious Injuries
"Employers must report serious injuries to the Labour Program within 24 hours." This requirement emphasizes the immediate notification obligation for incidents resulting in serious harm to employees. The 24-hour timeframe underscores the importance of prompt reporting for timely intervention and potential prevention of further incidents.

#### Written Investigation Reports
"Employers must also submit written investigation reports to the Labour Program, for all temporary and permanent disabling injuries, within 14 days of the occurrence." This outlines the mandatory submission of detailed investigation reports within a 14-day window following any temporary or permanent disabling injury. The report must adhere to the "Hazardous Occurrence Investigations Report – LAB1070" format, ensuring consistency and comprehensiveness of the information provided.

#### Annual Reports
"Employers must  submit three annual reports to the Labour Program: Employers Annual  Hazardous Occurrence Report, Employer Annual Harassment and Violence Occurrence  Report and the Work Place Committee Report." This mandates the submission of three specific annual reports to the Labour Program. These reports cover a range of occupational health and safety concerns, including hazardous occurrences, harassment and violence, and the activities of the Workplace Committee. The annual reporting requirement facilitates ongoing monitoring and analysis of workplace safety trends.

### Employer’s Duty Regarding Competent Person’s Report

#### Distribution of Competent Person’s Report
"The employer must provide a copy of the CP report to the  complainant, respondent (if an employee), and the WPHSC or representative." This specifies the mandatory distribution of the competent person’s report to key stakeholders. The report must be redacted to protect the identity of individuals involved, respecting any consent responses received.

#### Consultation with PHSC, WPHSC or HSR
"The employer must consult with the PHSC, WPHSC or HSR, as required by section  20.1 of the COHSR, regarding the implementation of recommendations contained in  the CP report to prevent a recurrence of WPV, to the extent reasonably  practicable, as per subsection 20.6(1) and paragraph 20.9(5)(c) of the COHSR.  These recommendations should be implemented as soon as practicable, but not  later than 90 days from the date the employer received the CP report, as per  subsection 20.6(2) of the COHSR." This details the employer’s obligation to consult with the relevant health and safety committees (PHSC, WPHSC, or HSR) regarding the implementation of recommendations from the competent person’s report. The implementation of these recommendations must occur as soon as reasonably possible, but no later than 90 days from receipt of the report. The employer must retain a copy of the CP report for review by an ODM.

### Employer Complaint Handling Process

#### Monthly Status Updates
"You should include the following information on the status  of the resolution process:  the process that is being followed the status on the review and update of the  workplace assessment the status on timelines for the selection and/or  hiring, if applicable, of a conciliator  the status on timelines for the selection and/or  hiring, if applicable, of an investigator the status of the investigation report, and  the status on implementing the recommendations  from the investigator’s report..." This outlines the required content for monthly status updates provided to the principal party and responding party. The updates must cover the progress of the resolution process, including the steps being taken, the status of workplace assessments, timelines for conciliator and investigator selection, the status of the investigation report, and the implementation of recommendations.

#### Investigator vs. Employer for Status Updates
"No, only the employer or designated recipient can provide  the monthly status updates." This clarifies that the responsibility for providing monthly status updates rests solely with the employer or designated recipient, not the investigator.

question: What factors does the Board consider when deciding whether to revoke the certification of a trade union or declare that a bargaining agent is no longer entitled to represent employees in a bargaining unit?
answer:
## Factors Considered by the Board When Deciding on Revocation or Declaration of Inability to Represent

### Application for Revocation of Certification

#### Majority of Employees No Longer Wishing Representation
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This section explicitly states the primary factor the Board considers when deciding whether to revoke certification. It highlights the Board's need to be
"...satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them..." This determination is made after an inquiry, which can take the form of a representation vote or other methods deemed appropriate by the Board. If this majority is found, the Board issues an order revoking the certification or declaring the bargaining agent no longer entitled to represent the employees.

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This subsection introduces an additional factor when no collective agreement is in force. It specifies that an order revoking certification cannot be made unless the Board is convinced that the bargaining agent has
"...failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit." This indicates that the Board assesses the bargaining agent's commitment to reaching a collective agreement as a crucial element in its decision-making process.

### Application for Declaration of Inability to Represent

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (When No Collective Agreement is in Force)
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This subsection reiterates the importance of the bargaining agent's efforts to reach a collective agreement when no existing one is in force. It clarifies that an order declaring the bargaining agent not entitled to represent employees cannot be made unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has
"...failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (When a Collective Agreement is in Force)
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union."

While not directly addressing the revocation of certification or declaration of inability to represent, this section touches upon the Board's consideration of a union's membership practices. It states that the Board may disregard membership requirements if the union has a history of admitting members without regard to the charter's stipulations. This suggests that the Board assesses the legitimacy and adherence to union rules as a factor in determining whether a union can legitimately represent employees.

#### Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement (During a Strike or Lockout)
"An application under subsection (1) or (3) must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made in respect of the bargaining agent for employees in a bargaining unit during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part."

This subsection addresses the Board's consideration of the bargaining agent's efforts to reach a collective agreement during a strike or lockout. It states that an application for revocation of certification or declaration of inability to represent cannot be made during a strike or lockout unless the Board consents. This implies that the Board assesses whether the bargaining agent has made a reasonable effort to reach a collective agreement despite the industrial action.

question: Under what circumstances can the Board decide not to file a copy of its order or decision in a court?
answer:
## Circumstances Where the Board May Not File a Copy of its Order or Decision in Court

### Section 23(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This section outlines the general obligation of the Board to file a copy of its order or decision in the Federal Court upon request. However, it provides two specific circumstances where the Board may decline to do so. 

The first circumstance is when the Board believes there is
"...no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision..." This suggests that if the Board has reason to believe that the employer will adhere to the order without further prompting, it may deem the filing in court unnecessary. 

The second circumstance is when the Board has
"...other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." This is a broader exception, allowing the Board to forgo filing if it perceives no practical benefit to doing so. The Board's "good reason" could encompass various factors, such as the order being self-executing or the potential for the order to be readily enforced through other means.



### Section 23(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding."

This section clarifies the procedure when the Board decides *not* to file in court. It states that the Board must inform the Court in writing that the filing is being made pursuant to subsection (1). This ensures transparency and allows the Court to understand the Board's rationale. However, it does not specify any other circumstances under which the Board may choose not to file in court.



### Section 22(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act."

This section emphasizes the finality of the Board's orders and decisions. It states that they are generally not subject to court review, except under very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act. This suggests that the Board has considerable discretion in deciding whether or not to file an order in court, and it is not obligated to do so in most cases.



### Section 156(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This section reiterates the finality of the Board's orders and decisions, echoing the sentiment expressed in Section 22(1). It reinforces the Board's discretion in deciding whether or not to file an order in court, as it is not required to do so in most instances.



In summary, the Board can decide not to file a copy of its order or decision in court under two main circumstances: when it has no indication of failure or likelihood of compliance with the order, or when it has other good reason why the filing in court would serve no useful purpose. However, the Board is generally obligated to file in court upon request, unless it has a valid reason not to do so. The finality of the Board's orders and decisions also gives the Board considerable discretion in this matter.

answer:
## Effect of Collective Agreement

### Section 56
"A collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit is, subject to and for the purposes of this Part, binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit and the employer."

This section directly addresses the effect of a collective agreement. It unequivocally states that such an agreement is "binding" on all parties involved: the bargaining agent, every employee within the bargaining unit, and the employer. The phrase
"...subject to and for the purposes of this Part..." indicates that the collective agreement operates within the framework of the Canada Labour Code and is intended to fulfill its objectives. This means that the terms of the collective agreement must comply with the provisions of the Code, and the agreement's effect is governed by the Code's rules and procedures.

question: What are the implications for a newly certified trade union in terms of initiating collective bargaining with an employer when it takes over as a party to an existing collective agreement?
answer:
## Implications for a Newly Certified Trade Union Initiating Collective Bargaining

### Section 36(1)(c): Substitution as a Party to Existing Collective Agreements

Section 36(1)(c) directly addresses the implications for a newly certified trade union when it assumes the bargaining agent role in an existing collective agreement. It states:
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

This passage is crucial because it clarifies the immediate effect of certification on existing collective agreements. When a new trade union is certified, it "is substituted" as a party to the existing agreement. This means that the previous bargaining agent is effectively removed from the agreement, and the newly certified union steps into their place.

### Section 36(2): Requirement to Commence Collective Bargaining

Section 36(2) outlines the trade union's right and obligation to initiate collective bargaining following certification, particularly when it becomes a party to an existing collective agreement. It specifies:
"Where, pursuant to paragraph (1)(c), a trade union is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section is significant because it grants the newly certified union the power to demand that the employer begin collective bargaining. The timeframe for this demand is within three months of certification. The union can request either a renewal or revision of the existing collective agreement or the negotiation of a completely new one. This ensures that the newly certified union has the opportunity to address the needs and concerns of the bargaining unit's employees.

### Section 36(3): Limitation on Subsection (2)

Section 36(3) provides a limitation on the requirement to commence collective bargaining outlined in subsection (2). It states:
"Subsection (2) does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1."

This passage is important because it excludes a specific type of certification from the three-month requirement to commence collective bargaining. A trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1 is not subject to this requirement. This suggests that the certification process under section 24.1 may have a different timeline or set of circumstances surrounding the initiation of collective bargaining.

question: What information must an employer provide to a bargaining agent when proposing a technological change that affects a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
answer:
## Section 52: Notice of Technological Change

### Contents of Notice
"The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)."

This section clearly outlines the mandatory information an employer must provide to a bargaining agent when proposing a technological change. The notice must be in writing and include a detailed description of the technological change itself, including its nature and proposed implementation date. Furthermore, the employer must estimate the number and type of employees likely to be affected, and articulate the anticipated impact on their terms and conditions of employment and job security. Finally, the employer is required to include any additional information specified in the regulations.

### Details of Proposed Change
"An employer who has given notice under subsection (1) to a bargaining agent shall, on request from the bargaining agent, provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out (a) a detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change; (b) the names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change; and (c) the rationale for the change."

This subsection elaborates on the employer's obligation to provide further details upon request from the bargaining agent. The employer must furnish a comprehensive description of the proposed technological change, including its specific nature. Additionally, the employer must identify the employees who are most likely to be initially impacted by the change. Crucially, the employer is also required to explain the reasoning behind the proposed technological change.

### Regulations
"The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Board, may make regulations (a) specifying the number of employees or the method of determining the number of employees that shall, in respect of any federal work, undertaking or business, be deemed to be “significant” for the purposes of subsections (1) and 54(2); and (b) requiring any information in addition to the information required by subsection (2) to be included in a notice of technological change."

This subsection grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations that further specify the information required in the notice of technological change. These regulations can define what constitutes a "significant" number of employees for the purposes of the notice and can mandate the inclusion of any additional information deemed necessary by the Board. This ensures that the bargaining agent receives a complete and informative picture of the proposed technological change.

question: What types of entities and their employees are subject to the provisions of this Part of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Entities and Their Employees Subject to This Part of the Canada Labour Code

### Crown Corporations

#### General Application to Crown Corporations
"This Part applies in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and in respect of the employees of any such corporation, except any such corporation, and the employees thereof, that the Governor in Council excludes from the operation of this Part." This section establishes the broad applicability of this Part to corporations established by the Government of Canada and their employees. However, it also includes an exception, allowing the Governor in Council to exclude certain Crown corporations from the Part's operation.

#### Application to Provincial Crown Corporations
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." This section specifically addresses provincial Crown corporations. It grants the Governor in Council the power to direct the Part's application to these corporations and their employees, provided they are agents of Her Majesty in right of a province and their activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

#### Application to Cooperatives
"For the purposes of section 251.18 and subsection 257(3), cooperatives shall be deemed to be corporations." This section clarifies the application of this Part to cooperatives. It states that cooperatives are to be treated as corporations for the purposes of sections 251.18 and 257(3) of the Canada Labour Code.

### Canadian Carriers
"This Part applies in respect of any Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and in respect of the employees of the carrier." This section extends the Part's application to Canadian carriers that are agents of Her Majesty in right of a province. It covers both the carriers themselves and their employees.

### Federal Work, Undertaking or Business Employers and Their Employees
"This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers." This section broadens the Part's application to employers who operate federal works, undertakings, or businesses and their employees. It covers the employers' relationships with their employees and trade unions and employers' organizations composed of those employees or employers.

### Other Corporations
"Section 5 (1) This Part applies in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and in respect of the employees of any such corporation, except any such corporation, and the employees thereof, that the Governor in Council excludes from the operation of this Part." This section reiterates the Part's application to corporations established for federal government functions and their employees, while again allowing the Governor in Council to make exceptions.

question: What is the approach taken for applying certain procedural requirements to regulations made under subsection 159(2) of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Application of Procedural Requirements to Regulations Made Under Subsection 159(2)

### General Approach

Section 160 outlines the approach taken for applying certain procedural requirements to regulations made pursuant to subsection 159(2) of the Canada Labour Code. It states,
"Subsections 121.2(3) to (8) apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of a regulation made pursuant to subsection 159(2) except that the references to “subsection (2)” in subsections 121.2(3) to (6) shall be read as references to subsection 159(2)."

This indicates that the procedural requirements detailed in subsections 121.2(3) to (8) are applicable to regulations made under subsection 159(2). However, it specifies a minor modification: any references to "subsection (2)" within those subsections should be interpreted as referring to subsection 159(2) instead. This ensures consistency in the application of the procedural requirements across different types of regulations made under the Canada Labour Code.

### Specific Procedural Requirements

The procedural requirements referenced in subsections 121.2(3) to (8) cover various aspects of the regulatory process. These include:

*   **Notification to the Minister:** Regulations made under subsection 159(2) must be notified to the Minister in the manner prescribed by subsection 121.2(3).
*   **Form and Content of Notices:** Regulations may prescribe the form and content of notices to be given by the Minister or other designated officers, as detailed in subsections 121.2(4) and (5).
*   **Time Limits and Board Jurisdiction:** Regulations may prescribe time limits for certain actions and rules regarding the Board’s jurisdiction, as outlined in subsection 121.2(6).
*   **Release of Reports:** Regulations may prescribe the manner in which reports of conciliation commissioners or boards may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute, as specified in subsection 121.2(8).

### Rationale for the Approach

The approach taken in section 160 is designed to maintain consistency and clarity in the application of procedural requirements across different types of regulations made under the Canada Labour Code. By modifying the references to "subsection (2)" in the applicable subsections, it ensures that the procedural requirements are correctly applied to regulations made under subsection 159(2). This approach promotes predictability and fairness in the regulatory process.

question: What role does the Minister play in the process of a trade union or employer giving notice of a potential strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## The Minister's Role in Strike and Lockout Notice

### Section 87.2: Notice to Employer and Trade Union

The Minister plays a crucial role in the process of a trade union or employer giving notice of a potential strike or lockout. Section 87.2 outlines the specific requirements for such notices and the Minister's involvement.
"...not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

This quote directly states that the Minister is required to receive a copy of a trade union's notice of a potential strike. This ensures that the Minister is informed of the impending action and can potentially intervene or facilitate resolution.
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

Similarly, this quote indicates that the Minister is also required to receive a copy of an employer's notice of a potential lockout. This further emphasizes the Minister's role in being kept informed of potential disruptions to operations.

### Section 87.3: New Notice

Section 87.3 addresses the scenario where a strike or lockout does not occur on the date indicated in a notice. It outlines the requirement for a new notice to be given.
"Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, where no strike or lockout occurs on the date indicated in a notice given pursuant to subsection (1) or (2), a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by the trade union or the employer if they wish to initiate a strike or lockout."

This quote highlights the Minister's role in receiving a copy of any new notice given after a previously announced strike or lockout has been averted. This ensures that the Minister remains aware of any changes in the potential for industrial action.

### Section 87.4: Maintenance of Activities

Section 87.4 details the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees during a strike or lockout. It also outlines the process for entering into an agreement regarding compliance with these obligations and the Minister's involvement.
"(2) An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose."

This quote states that an employer and trade union must enter into an agreement regarding compliance with the maintenance of activities obligations within 15 days of giving notice to bargain collectively. The Minister is required to receive a copy of this agreement.
"Immediately after entering into the agreement, the employer and the trade union must file a copy of it with the Minister and the Board."

This quote explicitly states that the employer and trade union must file a copy of the agreement with both the Minister and the Board. This ensures that the Minister is officially informed of the agreement and can potentially intervene or facilitate resolution.

### Section 87.5: Referral to the Board

Section 87.5 outlines the Minister's authority to refer any question with respect to the application of subsection (1) to the Board.
"The Minister may refer to the Board any question with respect to whether an agreement entered into by the employer and the trade union is sufficient to ensure that subsection (1) is complied with."

This quote directly states that the Minister has the power to refer any question regarding the sufficiency of an agreement to the Board. This allows the Board to make a determination on whether the agreement is adequate to prevent an immediate and serious danger to public safety or health.

### Section 87.6: Board Order

Section 87.6 details the Board's authority to issue an order to ensure compliance with the maintenance of activities obligations.
"If, in determining an application made under subsection (4) or referral made under subsection (5), the Board is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section."

This quote outlines the Board's power to issue an order to ensure compliance with the maintenance of activities obligations if it deems a strike or lockout to pose an immediate and serious danger to public safety or health. The Minister is informed of any such order through the filing of the agreement with the Minister and the Board.

question: Under what circumstances can an employee's complaint under the Canada Labour Code be suspended or not permitted?
answer:
## Suspension of Complaint

### Circumstances Leading to Suspension by the Board

Section 241.1 outlines the Board's power to suspend consideration of a complaint. It states:
"If the Board is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This indicates that the Board can suspend a complaint if it deems necessary for the complainant to take specific actions before the Board can proceed. These measures are detailed in section 241.1(2):
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures."

The suspension concludes when the Board is satisfied that the specified measures have been taken, as per section 241.1(3):
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

Similarly, Section 246.2 mirrors this power of suspension, stating:
"If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

### Circumstances Leading to Rejection of Complaint

Section 241.2 details the circumstances under which the Board may reject a complaint. It lists several reasons, including:
"(a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator; or (b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period."

This comprehensive list covers situations where the Board finds the complaint invalid, lacking merit, or already resolved through other means.

### Circumstances Preventing Complaint

Section 251.01 outlines the conditions under which an employee may make a complaint. It states:
"(1) Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Head if they believe that the employer has contravened (a) any provision of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part; or (b) any order."

However, it also specifies limitations on making a complaint. Section 251.01(3.1) prohibits an employee from making a complaint based on substantially the same facts as a complaint previously made under certain subsections, unless that prior complaint has been withdrawn. This prevents repetitive complaints on the same issues.

Furthermore, Section 251.01(5) provides a greater certainty regarding complaints related to collective agreements:
"For greater certainty, a complaint is not permitted under this section if it relates to a disagreement whose settlement is governed exclusively by a collective agreement under subsection 168(1.1)."

This clarifies that complaints about issues already covered by a collective agreement are not allowed under this section.

### Assistance from the Head

Section 251.03 describes the Head's power to assist parties to a complaint to settle it:
"After receipt of a complaint, the Head may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint."

This indicates that the Head can intervene to facilitate a resolution between the parties, potentially preventing the need for suspension or rejection of the complaint.

### Extension of Time

Section 251.03(3) grants the Head the power to extend the time period specified in the notice for the complainant to take necessary measures:
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice."

This provides flexibility for complainants who require additional time to fulfill the Board's requirements.

question: What are the implications for an employee and an employer in terms of contributions to benefits during an employee's leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Implications for Employee and Employer Contributions to Benefits During Leave of Absence

### Accumulation of Benefits During Leave

Section 209.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code states,
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave." This indicates a significant implication for both the employee and the employer. For the employee, it means that their benefits continue to accrue without interruption during the leave period. For the employer, it means that their contributions to these benefits continue as well, ensuring that the employee maintains their entitlements upon their return to work.

### Employee Responsibility for Contributions

Section 209.2(2) outlines the employee's responsibility for making contributions during a leave of absence. It says,
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (1), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any leave of absence under this Division unless, before taking leave or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." This implies that even during a leave of absence, the employee remains responsible for making contributions if required to maintain their benefits. However, the employee has the right to notify the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions, provided they do so reasonably in advance.

### Employer Responsibility for Contributions

Section 209.2(2.1) clarifies the employer's obligation to continue making contributions during a leave of absence. It states,
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (1) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s leave of absence under this Division in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not on leave unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time." This means that the employer's contributions to benefits continue at the same rate as if the employee were still working, unless the employee informs the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions within a reasonable timeframe.

### Failure to Pay Contributions

Section 209.2(3) addresses the consequences of the employee failing to pay contributions during a leave of absence. It says,
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (2) and (2.1), the benefits shall not accumulate during the leave of absence and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This indicates that if the employee does not pay their contributions, their benefits will not accumulate during the leave period, and their employment history will be considered continuous with their employment before the absence.

### Deemed Continuous Employment

Section 209.2(4) further clarifies the implications of failure to pay contributions on the calculation of benefits upon return to work. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating benefits of an employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division, other than benefits referred to in subsection (1), employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This means that even if the employee fails to pay their contributions during the leave, their employment history will be considered continuous with their employment before the absence for the purposes of calculating benefits upon their return.
