{"id": "CLC-213", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "DIVISION IX-Group Termination of Employment: Cooperation with Commission", "section": "213"}, "text": "Section 213 (1) An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee. Marginal note: Statement of benefits (2) An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 shall give each redundant employee, as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer. R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 213 1996, c. 11, s. 99 2018, c. 27, s. 575 Previous Version Marginal note: Establishment of joint planning committee"

question: What information must an employer provide to redundant employees in writing, and by when, after giving notice of termination under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Information to Provide Redundant Employees

### Required Written Information

According to Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code, an employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must provide each redundant employee,
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

This quote directly addresses the question by specifying the exact information that must be provided in writing. It details the categories of information required: vacation benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits and pay resulting from the employment. Furthermore, it sets a strict deadline for providing this information: no later than two weeks before the termination date.

### Timing of Provision

The Canada Labour Code clearly outlines the timeframe for providing this written statement. Section 213(2) states,
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee..." This indicates a two-week window from the date the notice of group termination is given to the Head. The employer must provide the statement as soon as practically possible within this timeframe, but the absolute latest is two weeks prior to the termination date.

### Additional Information Required

Section 213(1) further elaborates on the information that must be provided to the Canada Employment Insurance Commission. It states,
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee." This implies that the employer must proactively share any information requested by the Canada Employment Insurance Commission to aid the redundant employees in finding new work.

### Cooperation with Commission

Section 213(1) also mandates cooperation with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission. It specifies that the employer must
"...cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee." This highlights the employer's responsibility to work with the Commission to support the redundant employees in their job search.

Marginal note: Payment of amount and administrative fee (2) An employer or a director of a corporation is not permitted to request a review of a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the payment order and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the payment order in accordance with subsection 251.131(1), subject to, in the case of a director, the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18. Marginal note: Security (2.1) The Head may allow an employer or a director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (2). Marginal note: Review (3) On receipt of the request for review, the Head may, in writing, (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the payment order or the compliance order; or (b) confirm the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance, or rescind the notice, in which case the Head shall re-examine the complaint. Marginal note: Service of documents (4) Service of a decision made under subsection (3) shall be by personal service, by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation on any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance or, in the case of a compliance order, on the employer. If the decision is served by registered mail, it shall be deemed to have been received by the addressee on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed. Marginal note: Proof of service (5) A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head certifying that a decision referred to in subsection (4) was sent by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation to the addressee, accompanied by a true copy of the decision and by an identifying post office certificate of the registration or other proof, prescribed by regulation, that the decision has been sent or received, is admissible in evidence and is proof of the statements contained in the certificate, without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate. Marginal note: Review is final (6) Subject to the right of appeal under section 251.11, the decision made under subsection (3) is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court. Marginal note: Request treated as an appeal (7) The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12. 2012, c. 31, s. 225 2017, c. 20, s. 363 2018, c. 27, s. 599 Previous Version Marginal note: Appeal"

question: Can a request for review of a notice of violation be escalated to a higher authority, and under what circumstances?
answer:
## Escalation of a Notice of Violation Review

### Circumstances for Escalation

Yes, a request for review of a notice of violation can be escalated to a higher authority, specifically the Board. This escalation occurs when the Head considers the request to be an appeal.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal, in which case the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."

This passage explicitly states the condition under which a review request can be escalated. The Head has the discretion to treat the review request as an appeal. If the Head makes this determination, they must inform the applicant and forward the request to the Board. The Board then becomes the appellate body for the review.

### Process for Escalation

The process for escalating a review request to the Board involves the Head's decision to treat the request as an appeal.
"...the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."

This indicates that the Head initiates the escalation by informing the applicant and submitting the request to the Board. The Board then assumes the role of the appellate authority, reviewing the Head's decision.

### Alternative Escalation: Request for Review as an Appeal

Another circumstance for escalation is when the Head considers the request for review to be an appeal, even without explicitly being prompted to do so.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This passage highlights the Head's discretionary power to escalate a review request as an appeal. If the Head deems it appropriate, they will inform the relevant parties and forward the request to the Board, which then acts as the appellate body.

### Request for Review as an Appeal in Other Contexts

The possibility of treating a review request as an appeal also arises in other contexts within the Canada Labour Code.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This reiterates the Head's discretion to escalate a review request as an appeal, even if not explicitly requested. The Board then becomes the appellate body.

### Request for Review as an Appeal in Payment Order Reviews

The option to treat a review request as an appeal also applies to reviews of payment orders.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This passage confirms that the Head can escalate a review request as an appeal when considering a payment order. The Board then acts as the appellate authority.

Marginal note: Burden of proof (6) A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party. {"id": "CLC-6", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Application: Employees of Her Majesty | Presumption | Burden of proof", "section": "6"}, "text": "Section 6 Except as provided by section 5, this Part does not apply in respect of employment by Her Majesty in right of Canada. 1972, c. 18, s. 1 Marginal note: Presumption Section 6.1 (1) A person — other than a person who performs management functions or is employed in a confidential capacity in matters relating to industrial relations — who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer. Marginal note: Exception (2) The presumption does not apply for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part. 2024, c. 17, s. 235 Marginal note: Burden of proof Section 6.2 If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer. 2024, c. 17, s. 235"

question: In cases where an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, who bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did or did not occur?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Complaints Against Employers

### Section 133(6) of the Canada Labour Code
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This section directly addresses the question by establishing the burden of proof in complaints made to the Board. It states that the very fact of filing a complaint under section 133 serves as evidence that the alleged contravention *did* occur. Therefore, if a party to the complaint proceedings disputes this, the onus is on *that* party to prove that the contravention did *not* happen. This signifies a shift in the burden of proof when a complaint is lodged, placing it squarely on the employer to demonstrate the absence of the alleged violation.

### Section 133(6) and the Exercise of Rights

The quoted passage further clarifies the application of this burden of proof specifically when an employee exercises a right under sections 128 or 129. It emphasizes that the complaint itself is evidence of the contravention. Consequently, if an employer challenges the occurrence of the contravention, the employer bears the burden of proving that it did not happen. This underscores the protective nature of the complaint process, where the mere filing of a complaint provides a presumption of the employer's wrongdoing, requiring the employer to rebut that presumption.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

While this section doesn't specifically address complaints to the Board, it establishes a general rule regarding the burden of proof when an employer disputes an employee's status. It states that if an employer claims a person is not their employee in any proceeding other than a prosecution, the employer bears the burden of proving that the person is not their employee. This principle is consistent with the burden of proof established in section 133(6) for complaints to the Board, where the employer must prove the contravention did not occur if the employee files a complaint.

{"id": "LABOUR-STANDARDS-4_7", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Hours of work - Federally regulated workplaces", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Modified work schedule** Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work. Examples of modified work schedules include:   compressed work weeks flexible hours of work   Note: you can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements. For more information, please consult the Flexible Work Arrangements web page.  If you have a modified work schedule:   your standard hours of work for a period of 2 or more weeks cannot exceed an average of 40 hours in a week  the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed an average of 48 hours in a week your employer must pay overtime when  your daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule. Overtime must also be paid when your hours exceed an average of 40 hours in a week where the schedule consists of 2 or more weeks  If you are a student intern, your employer may establish a modified work schedule with your approval. This schedule can exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. However, it cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks.  **Requirements for creating, changing or canceling a modified work schedule** There are some requirements for creating, changing, or canceling a modified work schedule for one employee or a group of employees.  If you are covered by a collective agreement:  your employer and the union must agree to the modified work schedule in writing  If you are not covered by a collective agreement:   one employee or a group of employees must approve the modified work schedule:  				 for one employee, the schedule must be approved, in writing, by the affected employee and their employer for a group of employees, the schedule must be approved by at least 70% of the affected employees    For employees covered and not covered by a collective agreement, employers must post a notice of the new, revised or cancelled schedule at least 30 days before the schedule starts.  **Break, rest period, notice of work schedule and shift change** As an employee, and subject to the Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations, you are entitled to a break, rest period, notice of work schedule and notice of a shift change, as detailed below."

question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work for an employee in a week be adjusted or have exceptions?
answer:
## Conditions for Adjusting or Having Exceptions to Maximum Hours of Work

### Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This section outlines a primary condition under which the standard maximum hours can be adjusted. It states that employers can exceed the maximum hours in emergency situations, but this requires a report to the Head and, if applicable, the trade union within 15 days of the end of the month in which the employee(s) worked emergency hours. The report must detail the nature of the emergency, the number of employees working in excess of the maximum hours, and the number of additional hours each employee worked.

### Averaging
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks. As such, standard and maximum hours would be calculated across a period of 2 or more weeks rather than on a daily or weekly basis." This section describes another condition for adjusting maximum hours: averaging. It explains that in certain workplaces with irregular hours, employers can average an employee's hours over a period of two or more weeks. This means that the standard and maximum hours are calculated on a bi-weekly basis rather than a daily or weekly basis.

### Excess Hour Permit
"...the maximum hours of work can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit..." This point directly addresses an exception to the standard maximum hours. It states that employers can exceed the maximum hours under an excess hour permit, which is obtained in emergency situations.

### Averaging Plan

"For emergency work under an averaging plan." This further clarifies the application of averaging as an exception. It specifies that averaging plans can be used for emergency work.

### Modified Work Schedule
"...can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work under an averaging plan under a modified work schedule..." This section expands on the application of averaging as an exception, specifically mentioning its use in modified work schedules. It states that the maximum hours can be exceeded under an averaging plan within a modified work schedule.

### Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations
"As an employee, and subject to the Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations, you are entitled to a break, rest period, notice of work schedule and notice of a shift change, as detailed below." This refers to a set of regulations that provide further exemptions and modifications to the standard maximum hours. It indicates that employees are entitled to certain breaks and notices under these regulations.

### Specific Employee Classes
"Regulations set out exemptions from or modifications to what maximum hours of work is for certain classes of employees:  drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..." This section details specific employee classes that have exemptions or modifications to the standard maximum hours. It lists several examples, including truck drivers, ship employees in various regions, railway running trades employees, broadcasting commission salespersons, and banking commission-paid salespeople.
